title: Bhagat Singh Thind, 1923
hookLine: a Sikh army veteran is denied US citizenship by the Supreme Court

lines: A TURBAN AND AN ARMY UNIFORM.
ALL THE WAY TO THE SUPREME COURT.
cards: There's an old photograph of a young man in a United States Army uniform from the First World War. Stiff collar, straight back, and on his head, a turban. His name is Bhagat Singh Thind.
He came from Punjab to study and worked in lumber mills in Oregon to pay for college. When America went to war, he enlisted, served, and was honorably discharged.
Then he applied to become a citizen of the country he'd served, and his case went all the way to the Supreme Court.

teach.b: At the time, American law let only certain people become citizens by naturalization, and the key words were white persons. Thind was granted citizenship after the war, and the government fought it.
His lawyers argued that, by the science of the day, people from north India were counted in the same broad family as Europeans.

In February 1923, all nine justices ruled against him. Whatever the scientists said, they held, in the common understanding of ordinary people he was not white, and so could not be a citizen. The ruling hit hard.
Other Indian Americans had their citizenship taken away. Some lost land they had bought, because non-citizens couldn't own it in California.
Families who had built lives were told, in effect, you're guests here, not members.
Thind stayed. He kept teaching and writing, lecturing across America about the spiritual teachings of the Gurus and about finding the divine within.
A 1935 law opened citizenship to veterans of the First World War, and in 1936, in New York, he finally became a citizen. It took ten more years before Indians in general could. Now, his name.
Singh, lion, the name given to Sikh men with the Khalsa. A devoted lion, patient, and stubborn in the good way. The court said he didn't belong.

how: Sikh Americans remember Bhagat Singh Thind as a veteran and teacher, and his case is often taught in American history and civil-rights classes.

o: a devotee, someone devoted to God
a teacher who sings the Gurus' hymns
a soldier who has served with honor

games.q: you're Bhagat Singh Thind in 1923. the highest court in the land has just said you can't be a citizen. what do you do?
o: stay, keep teaching, and keep seeking citizenship.
stop wearing the turban to fit in.
games.why: he stayed, lectured across America on the Gurus' teachings, and became a citizen in 1936 through a law for war veterans.

practice: Think of a moment when someone was made to feel they didn't belong, at school, at work, online, in your family; maybe it was you. Picture it gently, then picture a different ending, where someone quietly says, they're with us.
Find the one sentence you could say to be that someone next time.

wordCard.voice: Bhagat. A devotee — the title behind the name of the Sikh veteran denied citizenship by the Supreme Court in 1923, who stayed, taught, and became a citizen in 1936.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: singh, lion; the name given to Sikh men at the founding of the Khalsa.

carryVoice: Your line: he belonged. A devoted lion, and in the end, a citizen. That's day three hundred seventeen.
